description: A fungal disease group that interferes with water movement through the plant and can cause progressive wilting.
symptoms: Wilting, yellowing, reduced growth, and discoloration of vascular tissue may occur; symptoms can progress even when soil has adequate moisture.
causes: Caused by soil-borne fungal pathogens that infect roots or vascular tissues.
favorable_conditions: Warm conditions, infected soil or planting material, poor sanitation, and repeated cropping can increase risk.
prevention: Use healthy planting material, maintain field sanitation, avoid moving contaminated soil, and use crop rotation where appropriate.
management: Remove severely affected plants, improve field hygiene, manage irrigation carefully, and use resistant varieties when available.
treatment: There is no single treatment for all fungal wilts. Use crop-specific, locally approved fungicides or biological/soil-management measures only when appropriate.

description: A broad term for diseases that produce dead or blighted areas on leaves.
symptoms: Brown, tan, or dark lesions on leaves that may enlarge and merge, followed by drying or premature leaf loss.
causes: May be caused by different fungal or bacterial pathogens depending on the crop.
favorable_conditions: High humidity, prolonged leaf wetness, poor air circulation, and infected crop debris can favor disease development.
prevention: Use clean seed or planting material, remove infected debris, improve airflow, and avoid unnecessary overhead irrigation.
management: Remove heavily affected material, maintain sanitation, manage irrigation, and use resistant varieties when available.
treatment: Treatment depends on the causal pathogen and crop. Use only crop-specific, locally approved products after diagnosis.

description: An insect pest problem in which caterpillars bore into fruits or other reproductive plant parts.
symptoms: Entry holes, frass near holes, internal feeding damage, premature fruit decay, and damaged or deformed fruits.
causes: Larvae of fruit-boring moths or other insects feed inside fruits.
favorable_conditions: Warm weather, susceptible crop stages, nearby host plants, and inadequate pest monitoring can increase infestations.
prevention: Scout regularly, remove damaged fruits, maintain field sanitation, use pheromone or light traps where suitable, and encourage natural enemies.
management: Monitor pest levels, remove infested fruits, conserve beneficial insects, and use integrated pest management practices.
treatment: If intervention is justified, use a crop- and pest-specific, locally approved insecticide according to its label and resistance-management guidance.

description: An insect pest problem in which larvae tunnel into stems and disrupt plant growth and transport.
symptoms: Wilting or drying shoots, dead hearts in young plants, stem holes, frass, weak stems, and reduced grain or fruit production.
causes: Larvae of stem-boring insects enter and feed within plant stems.
favorable_conditions: Warm conditions, continuous host availability, crop residue, and inadequate monitoring can favor infestation.
prevention: Use healthy planting material, remove or manage infested residues, rotate crops where appropriate, and monitor regularly.
management: Scout for early symptoms, remove severely infested plants when practical, conserve natural enemies, and use integrated pest management.
treatment: Use only crop-specific, locally approved insecticides or other controls when pest thresholds justify treatment.

description: A destructive blight disease that can rapidly damage foliage and fruit or tubers under favorable conditions.
symptoms: Water-soaked or dark lesions on leaves, rapid browning and collapse of foliage, and dark lesions on fruit or tubers.
causes: Caused by the oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans.
favorable_conditions: Cool to mild temperatures combined with high humidity, rain, fog, and prolonged leaf wetness favor epidemics.
prevention: Use healthy planting material, remove volunteer plants and infected debris, improve airflow, and avoid prolonged leaf wetness.
management: Scout frequently, remove infected material where feasible, manage irrigation, and follow local disease-management programs.
treatment: Preventive or early fungicide programs may be used where locally registered; rotate modes of action and follow the product label.

description: A vascular wilt disease caused by Fusarium species that can persist in soil and infect plant roots.
symptoms: Yellowing, one-sided or progressive wilting, stunting, and brown discoloration of vascular tissue may occur.
causes: Soil-borne Fusarium pathogens enter through roots and colonize vascular tissues.
favorable_conditions: Warm soil, susceptible varieties, contaminated soil or planting material, and repeated cultivation of host crops can increase risk.
prevention: Use resistant varieties where available, clean planting material, sanitation, crop rotation where effective, and avoid moving infested soil.
management: Remove severely affected plants, maintain sanitation, manage irrigation, and use resistant varieties or grafted material where appropriate.
treatment: Management is mainly preventive and integrated; crop-specific biological or chemical options should be selected using local recommendations.

description: A group of fungal diseases characterized by powdery fungal growth on plant surfaces.
symptoms: White or gray powdery patches on leaves, stems, or other plant parts, followed by yellowing, distortion, or premature aging.
causes: Caused by powdery mildew fungi that grow on plant surfaces.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures, humid air, dense canopies, and poor air circulation can favor disease development.
prevention: Provide adequate spacing and airflow, remove heavily infected material, and avoid excessive nitrogen that produces very dense growth.
management: Scout early, remove severely affected tissue, improve canopy ventilation, and use resistant varieties where available.
treatment: Registered fungicides or other approved products may be effective when applied early; rotate modes of action and follow labels.

description: A group of viral diseases that cause characteristic mosaic or mottled patterns and can reduce plant vigor and yield.
symptoms: Light and dark green mosaic patterns, mottling, leaf distortion, stunting, and reduced fruit or seed production.
causes: Caused by plant viruses that may spread through infected planting material, contact, tools, or insect vectors depending on the virus.
favorable_conditions: Infected seed or planting material, vector activity, contaminated tools, and susceptible crops can promote spread.
prevention: Use certified healthy planting material, remove infected plants, disinfect tools, control relevant vectors, and manage weeds that may host viruses.
management: Remove infected plants where appropriate, control vectors, maintain sanitation, and use resistant varieties when available.
treatment: There is no curative treatment for an infected plant. Management focuses on prevention, sanitation, vector control, and resistant varieties.

description: A disease complex that causes seeds or young seedlings to rot and collapse.
symptoms: Poor emergence, rotting seeds, water-soaked lesions at the stem base, seedling collapse, and rapid death.
causes: Often associated with soil- or water-borne pathogens including Pythium, Phytophthora, and Rhizoctonia species.
favorable_conditions: Overwatering, poor drainage, high humidity, overcrowded seedlings, and contaminated growing media favor disease.
prevention: Use clean seed and growing media, provide drainage, avoid overwatering, ensure ventilation, and avoid overcrowding.
management: Remove diseased seedlings, reduce excess moisture, improve drainage and airflow, and sanitize containers and tools.
treatment: Where registered, crop-specific seed treatments or fungicidal drenches may be used according to local recommendations and labels.

description: Leaf curling is a symptom rather than one single disease and may result from viruses, insects, environmental stress, or other causes.
symptoms: Upward or downward curling, puckering, distortion, yellowing, reduced leaf size, and sometimes stunting.
causes: Possible causes include viral infection, sap-sucking insects, heat or water stress, herbicide injury, and nutrient imbalance.
favorable_conditions: Conditions depend on the cause; vector activity, environmental stress, or exposure to damaging chemicals can contribute.
prevention: Use healthy planting material, monitor insect vectors, maintain appropriate irrigation and nutrition, and prevent spray drift.
management: Inspect plants and undersides of leaves, identify the underlying cause, remove severely affected plants when appropriate, and correct environmental stresses.
treatment: Treatment depends on the cause. Viral leaf curl has no curative treatment; control vectors and use resistant varieties where available.

description: A nutritional disorder caused by insufficient availability or uptake of one or more essential plant nutrients.
symptoms: Depending on the nutrient, plants may show chlorosis, necrosis, stunting, poor root growth, abnormal leaf coloration, or reduced yield.
causes: Low soil nutrient levels, unsuitable soil pH, nutrient lock-up, poor root health, or imbalanced fertilization can cause deficiency.
favorable_conditions: Very acidic or alkaline soils, poor soil structure, waterlogging, drought, and low nutrient availability can increase risk.
prevention: Use soil testing, balanced fertilization, appropriate pH management, organic matter management, and good root-zone conditions.
management: Confirm the suspected nutrient deficiency with soil or plant analysis where possible, then correct the specific nutrient imbalance.
treatment: Apply the deficient nutrient at a crop-appropriate rate based on soil or plant testing and local fertilizer recommendations.

description: A root disease complex in which roots decay, reducing water and nutrient uptake.
symptoms: Wilting, yellowing, stunting, poor vigor, dark or soft roots, and root tissue decay.
causes: Can be caused by several soil-borne fungi or oomycetes, often associated with excessive soil moisture.
favorable_conditions: Waterlogged or poorly drained soil, overirrigation, compacted soil, and infected planting material can favor root rot.
prevention: Improve drainage, avoid overwatering, use healthy planting material, sanitize growing media, and use resistant varieties where available.
management: Improve drainage and irrigation practices, remove severely affected plants, and maintain root-zone sanitation.
treatment: Treatment depends on the pathogen and crop; use only locally registered products or biological measures appropriate for the confirmed cause.

description: A group of oomycete diseases that commonly cause leaf lesions and downy growth under humid conditions.
symptoms: Yellow or pale angular leaf spots, brown lesions, and gray, white, or purplish downy growth on leaf undersides may occur.
causes: Caused by downy mildew oomycetes that produce spores under favorable environmental conditions.
favorable_conditions: Cool to moderate temperatures, high humidity, rain, and prolonged leaf wetness favor infection and spread.
prevention: Improve airflow, avoid unnecessary overhead irrigation, use healthy planting material, and remove infected debris.
management: Scout early, reduce leaf wetness, improve canopy ventilation, and follow local disease-management recommendations.
treatment: Where registered, fungicides or oomycete-targeted products may be used preventively or early; rotate modes of action and follow labels.

description: A bacterial vascular disease that can cause rapid wilting while leaves may initially remain green.
symptoms: Sudden wilting, drooping leaves, vascular discoloration, and sometimes bacterial streaming from cut stems.
causes: Caused by bacterial pathogens that colonize vascular tissues and may survive in soil or plant material.
favorable_conditions: Warm conditions, wet soil, contaminated planting material, infected soil, and movement of contaminated water or tools can increase spread.
prevention: Use healthy planting material, sanitation, resistant varieties where available, crop rotation where effective, and avoid moving contaminated soil or water.
management: Remove affected plants, sanitize tools, manage irrigation and drainage, and control sources of contaminated soil or water.
treatment: There is generally no reliable curative treatment for an infected vascular plant; management focuses on sanitation, resistance, and prevention.

description: A dark superficial fungal growth that commonly develops on honeydew deposited by sap-sucking insects.
symptoms: Black, soot-like coating on leaves, stems, or fruit surfaces; heavy growth can reduce light interception and photosynthesis.
causes: Fungi grow on sugary honeydew produced by insects such as aphids, whiteflies, and scale insects.
favorable_conditions: High populations of honeydew-producing insects and humid conditions favor development.
prevention: Monitor and manage the underlying insect infestation, encourage natural enemies, and maintain good plant hygiene.
management: Control the honeydew-producing pest using integrated pest management; the mold usually declines once honeydew production stops.
treatment: Treat the underlying insect problem rather than the mold alone. Use locally approved pest-control products when necessary.

description: A group of fungal diseases that produce characteristic rust-colored spore-producing lesions.
symptoms: Orange, yellow, brown, or reddish pustules on leaves or stems, sometimes followed by yellowing and premature leaf loss.
causes: Caused by rust fungi that produce spores and may require specific host plants or environmental conditions.
favorable_conditions: High humidity, leaf wetness, moderate temperatures, and susceptible plant varieties can favor infection.
prevention: Use resistant varieties, maintain airflow, remove volunteer hosts where appropriate, and manage crop debris according to local recommendations.
management: Scout regularly, remove severely affected material where practical, and follow local rust-management programs.
treatment: Registered fungicides may be useful for some crops when applied at the correct stage; follow local labels and rotate modes of action.

description: An insect pest problem caused by tiny thrips that feed by rasping and sucking plant tissues.
symptoms: Silvery or bronzed leaf areas, distorted young leaves, flower damage, scarring, black fecal spots, and poor fruit quality.
causes: Thrips feed on leaves, flowers, and developing fruits; some species can also transmit plant viruses.
favorable_conditions: Warm, dry conditions, flowering crops, weeds, and protected plant environments can support populations.
prevention: Scout flowers and young leaves, control weeds, use reflective or physical barriers where suitable, and conserve beneficial insects.
management: Use integrated pest management with monitoring, sanitation, biological control, and selective treatments when thresholds are reached.
treatment: Use only locally registered insecticides for the specific crop and thrips species; rotate modes of action to reduce resistance.

description: Aphids are small sap-sucking insects that can weaken plants and may transmit plant viruses.
symptoms: Clusters of small insects on tender growth, curled or distorted leaves, yellowing, sticky honeydew, and sooty mold.
causes: Aphids colonize young shoots and undersides of leaves and reproduce rapidly under favorable conditions.
favorable_conditions: Tender new growth, moderate temperatures, excess nitrogen, and limited natural-enemy activity can favor aphid outbreaks.
prevention: Inspect new growth, manage weeds, avoid excessive nitrogen, and conserve ladybirds, lacewings, parasitoids, and other natural enemies.
management: Monitor populations, use physical removal for small infestations, conserve natural enemies, and use selective controls when necessary.
treatment: If treatment is justified, use a crop-specific, locally approved insecticide and follow resistance-management and label directions.

description: A group of bacterial diseases that cause discrete leaf spots and can reduce photosynthetic area.
symptoms: Small water-soaked or dark spots that may enlarge, become brown, develop yellow halos, and sometimes cause leaf drop.
causes: Caused by plant-pathogenic bacteria that spread through infected seed or plant material, rain splash, irrigation, tools, or handling.
favorable_conditions: Warm, humid weather, frequent rain, prolonged leaf wetness, and dense plantings favor disease spread.
prevention: Use clean seed and planting material, avoid working in wet crops, sanitize tools, improve airflow, and manage irrigation.
management: Remove severely infected material, reduce leaf wetness, maintain sanitation, and use resistant varieties where available.
treatment: Copper or other bactericidal products may be registered for some crop-disease combinations; effectiveness varies, so follow local recommendations and labels.

description: Whiteflies are small sap-sucking insects that weaken plants, produce honeydew, and can transmit viruses.
symptoms: Small white insects on leaf undersides, yellowing, leaf weakening, sticky honeydew, sooty mold, and possible virus symptoms.
causes: Whiteflies feed on plant sap and reproduce rapidly on suitable host plants.
favorable_conditions: Warm weather, dense vegetation, weeds, and protected cultivation can favor population growth.
prevention: Monitor leaf undersides, manage weeds and crop residues, use insect-proof barriers where suitable, and conserve natural enemies.
management: Use integrated pest management with monitoring, biological control, sanitation, and selective treatments when thresholds are exceeded.
treatment: Use only locally approved insecticides for the specific crop and whitefly species, and rotate modes of action to slow resistance.
